title: Double Negatives in Spanish: No Veo Nada Is Correct
seo_title: Double Negatives in Spanish: No Veo Nada Is Correct
meta_description: Double negatives in Spanish are correct and required: no veo nada, no viene nadie. Rules for nada, nadie, nunca, ninguno, ni and tampoco, plus a quiz.
excerpt: In English it’s a mistake. In Spanish, it’s the rule.

body_html:
Double negatives in Spanish are not a mistake; they are required. Where English says “I don’t see anything” (or, informally, “I don’t see nothing”, which teachers correct), Spanish says No veo nada, literally “I don’t see nothing”. Learners often avoid this because it feels wrong, and end up with No veo algo, which is incorrect. Here’s how negative words work in Spanish, with the one simple rule that governs them all.

Key takeaways
  • If a negative word comes after the verb, put no before the verb: No viene nadie.
  • If the negative word comes before the verb, drop no: Nadie viene.
  • Use negative words, not algo/alguien, in negative sentences: No quiero nada.
  • Several negatives can stack: No digo nunca nada a nadie.
{{toc}}

The negative words

PositiveNegativeExample
algo (something)nada (nothing, anything)No tengo nada.
alguien (someone)nadie (nobody, anybody)No conozco a nadie.
siempre / alguna veznunca, jamás (never, ever)No voy nunca.
alguno (some, any)ninguno (none, no, any)No tengo ningún problema.
también (also)tampoco (neither, either)No voy tampoco.
o… o (either… or)ni… ni (neither… nor)No bebo ni café ni té.

The RAE’s Nueva gramática calls this “negative concord”: negative words after the verb require a preceding negation.

Double negatives in Spanish: the position rule

Negative word after the verb: add no

  • No he visto a nadie. I haven’t seen anyone.
  • No como nunca carne. I never eat meat.
  • No quiero nada. I don’t want anything.

Negative word before the verb: no “no”

  • Nadie me ha llamado. Nobody has called me.
  • Nunca como carne. I never eat meat.
  • Nada es imposible. Nothing is impossible.

Both orders are correct; putting the negative word first sounds a bit more emphatic. What you can’t do is put it first and add no: Nadie no viene is wrong.

{{image:2}}

Ninguno: agreement and shortening

Ninguno agrees with the noun and shortens to ningún before a masculine singular noun: ningún libro, ninguna idea. It is almost always singular, even where English uses a plural: No tengo ningún amigo allí (I don’t have any friends there). As a pronoun: —¿Cuántos tienes? —Ninguno.

Nadie and the personal a

When nadie or alguien is the direct object, it takes the personal a: No veo a nadie, ¿Conoces a alguien?. See {{link:spanish-preposition-mistakes|Spanish preposition mistakes}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Stacking several negatives

Spanish happily stacks negatives, which English never allows:

  • No le digo nunca nada a nadie. I never tell anyone anything.
  • Nunca he visto nada parecido. I’ve never seen anything like it.
  • No quiero ni verlo. I don’t even want to see him.

Ni, ni siquiera and tampoco

  • No tengo ni tiempo ni dinero. I have neither time nor money.
  • Ni siquiera me saludó. He didn’t even say hello.
  • Yo tampoco lo sé. I don’t know either. See {{link:tambien-vs-tampoco|también vs tampoco}}.

Why this happens

English schools teach that two negatives make a positive, so “I don’t want nothing” is marked wrong. Learners bring that rule into Spanish and replace nada with algo: No quiero algo. To a Spanish speaker, that sounds like “I don’t want a particular something”, which is odd. In fact, many languages, including French, Italian and Portuguese, use negative concord; English is the unusual one. Once you accept that Spanish negatives agree with each other rather than cancel out, the pattern feels natural.

Useful everyday expressions

  • De nada. You’re welcome (literally “of nothing”).
  • Nada más. Nothing else / That’s all.
  • Nunca jamás. Never ever.
  • Ni idea. No idea.
  • Ni hablar. No way.
  • Como si nada. As if nothing had happened.

Several of these use a negative word without no, because the negative word stands alone or comes first, exactly as the position rule predicts.

Also note that sin (without) works like a negative: Salió sin decir nada a nadie (He left without saying anything to anyone).

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
No veo algo.No veo nada.Negative sentence: nada
No conozco alguien.No conozco a nadie.Nadie + personal a
Nadie no vino.Nadie vino.Negative first: no no
No tengo ningunos amigos.No tengo ningún amigo.Ninguno is singular
Veo nadie.No veo a nadie.Negative after the verb needs no
{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. I don’t need anything. (No necesito nada.)
  2. Nobody knows. (Nadie lo sabe.)
  3. I’ve never been to Cuba. (No he estado nunca en Cuba. / Nunca he estado en Cuba.)
  4. There isn’t any problem. (No hay ningún problema.)
  5. She doesn’t eat fish or meat. (No come ni pescado ni carne.)

All mistake types in {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|my guide to common Spanish mistakes}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

In Spanish, negatives agree. Negative word after the verb? Put no in front. Negative word first? Leave no out. And swap algo, alguien, alguno for nada, nadie, ninguno in negative sentences. That’s all there is to it.

faq.q: Are double negatives correct in Spanish?
faq.a: Yes. Spanish requires them: No veo nada (I don’t see anything), No viene nadie (Nobody is coming).

faq.q: Is it no veo algo or no veo nada?
faq.a: No veo nada. In negative sentences, Spanish uses nada, nadie and ninguno instead of algo, alguien and alguno.

faq.q: When do you not need no with nadie or nunca?
faq.a: When the negative word comes before the verb: Nadie viene, Nunca bebo café.

questions.explain: Ninguno is singular and shortens to ningún.
Negative after the verb needs no.
